story_text.value:
Hi Hacker News,

I present to you "Lunchtime Broadcast", a walkaround-game (in the vein of Homestuck) where the mechanics are primarily walking your character around and talking to people in order to advance the plot. It's set in a fictional Korean high school, where you learn part of the vocabulary used in the webtoon "Sora & Haena!".

I am a big believer in comprehensible input, and so I had Claude come up with its own original story that teaches vocab from the webtoon's first 4 episodes, but is targeted to my intermediate-ish level. The hope is that after playing through "Lunchtime Broadcast", reading the webtoon should be much easier for me.

Notable Features :

- Built for phones but playable on desktop

- Every word in the dialogue is tappable and gives a definition Claude wrote in simpler Korean. English definitions are hidden behind a "?" icon

- There is a dictionary that shows words by how often or how recently you have tapped them

- Words that have been taught come up as multiple choice cloze review questions when you talk to characters. Many scenes have unique questions that use and quiz the taught vocabulary, even vocab from previous chapters

- As players progress, they unlock some culture and grammar notes (which I had Claude generate and then fact-check against online sources)

The development process (ongoing) involves me having Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.1 Sol play through the chapters multiple times as a player in polishing passes, as well as feedback from me as I played through. I have currently only played completely through chapters 1 and 2, but there are 4 game chapters. The Korean lines were generated by Claude, not by native speakers, so there may be mistakes.

Repo: https://github.com/Stan-Stani/jeomsim-bangsong

Live Game: https://stan-stani.github.io/jeomsim-bangsong/

title.value: Show HN: Vibecoded top-down game for learning vocab from a Korean webtoon

story_text.value:
I think a chasm has been crossed. Opus 5.5 few shotted a fully working Figma for me. In the past year I have been trying to benchmark vibe coded apps and see how good they get and this week it did it with very very little guidance from me. I basically just told it reach feature parity.

Prior to this vibe coded apps would resemble the real software, this is not a resemblance it's the real thing. As a casual Figma user in the past, I can't really see a difference. And if there is one you have an LLM that can on the fly operate the app or use it.

P.S. I did this is on Mana which is our startup making it easier for LLMs to do it (probably the code is half of what would have been and there are primitives it can use but ultimately it's a testament to how good models have gotten). I went on to make google meets, docs, telegram, linear, etc. All basically with single prompts. The biggest jump has been in the UX understanding of models and attention to detail.

title.value: Show HN: Opus 5.5 made a fully featured Figma clone in 3 hours / 8 prompts

story_text.value:
https://loglinealign.com/

I vibe-coded an application that merges entries from multiple log files into a single, chronologically ordered view. It handles timezone offsets and can auto-detect some timestamp formats, with an option to specify the format manually.

Files are processed on your device and not uploaded to a server.

It's all open source: https://github.com/jftuga/loglinealign

In the repo, there is a quick, 3 minute narrated explainer video as well as a CLI version.

Also, lnav does the same thing in a TUI and is more capable.

story_text.value:
I've been a photographer for decades, and for a long time I've wanted to make an app that will tell me when the sun's light will directly hit the/a surface of a building.

This weekend I found the time to build and launch a thing that does that. Features include:

  - Enter an address, get back a map with calendar details and some dataviz on when the sun is going to hit each wall

  - Save buildings, walls, and dates in a Planner, with a Calendar feed

  - Analyze the sun between two points along a street (currently limited to 5km along a single street)

  - Share links to what you've found
Sources used include: OpenStreetMap, Nominatim, Photon and the US Census Bureau geocoder. Sun positions come from the NOAA solar position algorithm, computed in-browser. Cloud forecasts from Open-Meteo.

I hope you find it useful, and welcome feedback!

story_text.value:
The Enso Method is a new set of AI skills for Claude Code and Codex which I've open sourced on GitHub predominantly for developers who build for someone else who is making the product/business calls.

I've been using AI to write basically 100% of my code since late 2024, back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, when it barely worked and there were few people doing this and very little support for this way of developing. I stubbornly thought this was going to be the future and came up with a methodology for making it work, before "AI skills" were even a thing. Since then I've continued to refine the method and I just recently published it as open source. The method focuses on requirements (PRD, TDD) up front, and has skills that autonomously refine the requirements, declaring assumptions that should be validated by stakeholders. It doesn't expect you to be a solo founder or that whoever is at the keyboard directing Claude or Codex to be the product owner and business decider in addition to being the developer. I think most of us sit in the seat where we develop for someone else who decides. And if AI is all about velocity, then if we have to slow down to get product owners to review and decide, that puts a serious damper on the efficiency everyone expects from AI development. So a defining attribute of the Enso Method is, when it reviews the requirements prior to implementation, it asks what questions/gaps there are and it tries to answer its own questions. If it can get to 95%+ confidence in the answers, it just rolls with those. If less then it will declare the assumption in an assumptions.md file which gets routed to business stakeholders to review. In the meantime however we still consider this to be a green light, we can move forward and implement with the assumptions, and if we later hear from the business that the assumption was wrong, we update the requirements and re-implement, because implementation is now cheap, and waiting isn't.

title.value: Show HN: Enso Method – agent skills for building software for someone else

story_text.value:
I've been working on this app for a couple months, because I needed help outlining my story being written on Google Docs.

I kept adding new characters, and it was difficult for me to keep track of everything going on in the story. I wasn't organized at all.

I do have a subscription to Claude, and it helps, sure, but it didn't exactly build a graph of all the story elements connecting together. Throwing 20 chapters into one context was just terrible at narrowing its focus.

I started building this tool as a way to help me with a few things...

First, was replace Google Docs, because that thing lagged like crazy after 20~ chapters.

Second, was scanning my chapters. I wanted to automate creating a graph of characters, places, factions, objects, monsters, everything. I even started mapping out plots, threads, promises, and events. I threw it all into a database, and am able to lay it all out on the table, in an easy to absorb format.

Want to see where someone traveled throughout the story? What about when they encountered others? Well, now I can! Replacing names and all their aliases throughout the whole book? Easy peasy. What about fixing plot holes? No problem, we can fix those too.

Anyways, I took the extra effort to make it available for everyone by throwing it on on k3s and building the extra framework around the workspace.

It's completely free to use. Scanning chapters requires AI credits, which you get 50 for free at signup. Enough to scan about 15 chapters, or start a new story.

If you need more credits, let me know and I'll gift you more.

title.value: Show HN: Authrot – extract your story elements out of chapters and graph them

I got sick of seeing my various family members playing solitaire games with ads or subscriptions, and it's 2026 where you can just ask for software, which makes it all the more frustrating that the classic games got enshittified, so I made this. I have put a fair bit of effort into the UI, rules, and bots for games that I personally know well. But of course I haven't played all these games in real life, and so some may have rules or UI issues that I will need feedback to resolve.
